Access and usage limits

Confirm before ordering: Package access, downloads and update eligibility.

Ask SEOGBTools support to confirm what your plan includes and whether any usage caps apply.

Pillbanana lists WordPress themes and plugins. If you are evaluating a listing, check which version is included, where updates come from, and what support is available. A site owner choosing a theme for a shop should also check that the theme handles product pages, checkout, and mobile navigation well.

Check compatibility on staging

Confirm the supported WordPress, PHP, and WooCommerce versions. Test the package on a staging copy first. Open key pages as a visitor, check the checkout flow in test mode where relevant, and make sure existing plugins still behave as expected.

Verify update sources

Check who supplies releases and whether an account or key is needed for updates or premium services. Keep a record of the source and version you install. Compare Pillbanana's catalog with the developer's own documentation before selecting a package.

Compare package, updates, and support

A theme can appear to offer the layout you need while depending on a separate builder or add-on. Write down those dependencies before comparing the package with the developer’s own offer. Check what an update requires and who can help if a version conflicts with your store. Test a representative product and category page on staging, including the mobile menu and search. Record the version, the tested environment, and a rollback path so the person maintaining the site can repeat the check after an update.

Start with the pages your site needs

Before browsing Pillbanana or another WordPress catalog, write down which pages need to work on launch day. An online store might need a homepage, a category page, a product page, a cart, and a checkout. A service business might need a service page, a booking form, and a contact page. Test themes against those pages first. A demo built around a portfolio can look polished while leaving the layout for your most important page unclear.

List the parts visitors need to use. On a product page, they may need to switch between variations, read delivery information, and add the right item to the cart. On a booking page, they may need to choose a time and receive a confirmation. Include the tasks your team performs behind the scenes too, such as changing a price, updating opening hours, or adding a photo without touching code.

Decide which layout details matter enough to influence your choice. If a store has long product names, check whether they wrap properly on small screens. If your business relies on local visits, make sure phone and address links are easy to find. A few clear tasks give you a better basis for comparison than a long feature list.

Compare WordPress themes using your own content

Create a small set of test content that resembles what you plan to publish. Include a long heading, a short heading, several product photos, and one page with a form. Use the same material for each theme you compare. That way you can see whether a difference comes from the theme or from the carefully chosen content in its demo.

Check how the theme handles content when the screen is narrow. Open the homepage and navigate to a product using the mobile menu. Try reading product details, changing a variation, and opening the cart. Look for text that wraps awkwardly or buttons that become hard to reach. If an important step needs a custom layout, record the work it would take to build and maintain it.

Ask what the demo needs to look the way it does. Some designs depend on a page builder, extra plugins, or demo images. Make a list of the dependencies you would use and check who supplies them. If you only need the basic layout, you may be able to skip several extras. Fewer dependencies can make it easier to understand which component controls a page when you need to update it.

Check how you would leave the theme later. Your store's products and order records should remain accessible through the tools that manage them, but layouts or design blocks can depend on a particular builder. Test how a representative page looks after switching themes on staging. A small test can show which pages would need rebuilding before you commit to a design across the whole site.

Give every plugin a clear job

Write one sentence describing what each plugin must do. For a contact form, you might need visitors to select a service, send a message, and receive an acknowledgement. For a store, you might need to collect a delivery note and show it to staff when they prepare the order. Clear requirements make it easier to compare options and notice when an existing plugin already handles the task.

Review overlapping features before installing a second tool. If two plugins can add product filters, decide which one owns the filter interface and which settings you need. Duplicate functions can make it hard to tell which setting is responsible when something changes. Keep a simple record of which plugin handles forms, search, caching, and other parts of the site you expect to maintain.

Check who will manage the plugin after launch. A plugin that requires a developer to edit settings may still make sense if those settings rarely change. If staff need to use it every day, test the workflow with someone who will actually run it. Ask them to complete the task with a sample record and note which steps caused confusion.

Verify compatibility on a staging site

Check the supported versions of WordPress, PHP, and WooCommerce before you install a package. Use a staging copy that resembles the live site. A blank demo installation can miss problems caused by the mix of plugins and settings your real site uses. Keep the staging site separate from live customers and use test settings for any services that send messages or take payments.

Start with one change at a time. Install the theme or plugin, activate it, and repeat your short test list. On a shop, open a product, try a variation, add it to the cart, and use the checkout in test mode. On a service site, submit a test enquiry and check that the right notification arrives. Try both logged-in and public views where those views affect the workflow.

Check admin tasks as well as public pages. Edit a sample product and reopen it to see whether your changes were saved. Try updating a page with the editor your staff use. If the plugin adds information to an order or submission, confirm that the people who need the information can find it. A feature is only useful if the whole task works from the visitor's action to the staff member's next step.

Keep a test record. Write down the package version, the environment, what worked, and any issue you need to investigate. A note like “delivery note visible at checkout but missing from the staff order view” gives a developer a specific problem to reproduce. When you change a setting or try another package, repeat that same test and record the new result.

Compare the package with the developer's offer

A listing can describe a theme or plugin without making clear which services come with it. Check the package contents, the version, and where the files come from. Then compare those details with the developer's documentation. You may find that a demo library, support service, or cloud feature uses a separate account. If you need one of those features, confirm access before you depend on it.

Ask what the seller supplies when an update comes out. You may be able to install a package manually while automatic updates require a connection to the developer's service. Record which method is available and how you will find out that an update exists. A lower upfront price can lead to more maintenance work if someone has to check versions and apply updates manually.

Compare support arrangements for your likely problems. If a theme changes your checkout layout or a plugin stops sending a form notification, who can help you diagnose it? Some site owners handle troubleshooting themselves. Others need a support contact they can reach quickly. Check which option fits the people who will maintain the site after launch.

Keep an update and rollback record

Write down the installed version and where you got it. Keep the date of the last staging test and the version of the tools that depend on the package. This record helps when a teammate needs to investigate why one site behaves differently from another. It also gives you a way to spot when a package has gone a long time without an update.

Before a change reaches the live site, check that you can restore the previous working setup. Keep the backup and instructions where the person responsible for the site can find them. If the update changes stored settings or data, make sure the rollback plan accounts for that. Test the recovery procedure on staging when practical so you know what it requires.

Repeat the checks that matter to your site after an update. For the store example, confirm that visitors can still choose the right variation, see the expected delivery options, and complete a test checkout. For a service site, check that enquiries and confirmations still arrive. Use the same test tasks each time so you can detect a change in behavior without relying on a general impression.

Work through one example before choosing a package

Suppose a small store wants to refresh its product pages. The owner wants larger photos, clear variation controls, and a better place to explain delivery. The team can shortlist two themes and build one sample product in each. They can test the same long product name, the same set of variations, and the same delivery information on both.

During testing, the first theme makes the photos easy to browse but needs a builder for the delivery section. The second can show the delivery section with its own controls but takes more work to set up the image layout. The team can compare how long both tasks take and which dependencies they would have to maintain. They can also ask the person who updates products to edit the test page in both setups.

This comparison gives the owner a specific reason to choose. If staff update delivery information often, a simple editor may be more valuable than a gallery that looks slightly better. If the store sells products people inspect closely, the photo experience may matter more. Keep the test results and use them when you decide what to buy.

Check what is included before choosing access

Review the current Pillbanana listing for the exact package and compare it with the vendor's documentation. Check the versions offered, update arrangements, and any account requirements for services you need. If the package depends on a particular plugin, confirm that you can obtain and maintain that dependency. Check the Pillbanana catalog and browse the SEOGBTools shop for related resources.

A useful final comparison includes the package cost, the cost of any services you need separately, and the time someone will spend testing updates. Include the staff tasks and customer pages that matter most. Choose the package when you have enough evidence that it fits those tasks and that the maintenance process works for your team.

Frequently asked questions

What should I compare first when choosing a theme? Compare the pages customers use most and the tasks your staff perform. Use the same sample content on each theme so you can see which differences matter in practice.

Does a theme demo show everything I receive? Check the listing and vendor documentation for the included files, plugins, templates, and media. Ask which demo features require a separate service or account.

Can I test a plugin without changing the live site? Use a staging copy with representative settings and test data. Repeat the tasks that depend on the plugin and check the parts of the site that might be affected.

How do I check whether a package will receive updates? Ask who supplies updates, how you learn a new release is available, and what the installation process requires. Record those details beside the version you install.

When is a direct vendor plan worth comparing? Compare it when you need automatic updates, support, access to a connected service, or a feature tied to an account. Check the current terms and decide which of those services your site relies on.
